query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, a microstructure that features a refined grain architecture with continuous, protective intergranular oxide or intermetallic precipitates mediates both wear resistance (via strain hardening and grain boundary reinforcement) and corrosion resistance (via formation of a stable passive film).
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy synthesized via powder metallurgy/spark plasma sintering that exhibits a dual-phase microstructure with a body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution matrix and some intergranular precipitates (e.g., Laves phases and oxides).
generation.intervention: Alter the processing/sintering temperature to tailor the grain size and the continuity/amount of grain-boundary precipitates. For instance, comparing samples sintered at a lower temperature (yielding finer grains and a more continuous protective precipitate network) with those sintered at a higher temperature (giving coarser grains and less continuous precipitate distribution).
generation.conditions: Testing should be performed under combined mechanical abrasion (wear) and corrosive attack (e.g., in an acidic electrolyte) to simulate harsh environmental conditions. Measurements of wear depth and corrosion current/density should be recorded.
generation.structural_mediator: The grain boundaries reinforced by precipitated oxides and/or intermetallic phases (such as Laves phases) which can act as barriers to crack propagation during mechanical wear and as sites for forming a stable passive layer that limits corrosive degradation.
generation.mechanism: The mechanically refined grain structure increases the alloy’s strength through grain-boundary strengthening while the presence of intergranular precipitates (e.g., oxides) supports the formation and maintenance of a protective passive layer. Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, this integrated microstructure reduces material loss by both resisting mechanical deformation and lowering electrochemical attack rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The sample with a finely grained, continuous intergranular oxide/intermetallic network is expected to show lower wear rates and reduced corrosion current densities compared to a baseline alloy having a coarser microstructure with discontinuous or fewer protective precipitates.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy of the same nominal composition processed under conditions that result in coarser grains and reduced or discontinuous grain boundary precipitation, offering only a baseline level of wear and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold when the mechanical loads and corrosive conditions are within moderate extremes where the protective layer can form and remain intact. If mechanical stresses exceed the adhesion strength of the protective layer or if the corrosive environment disrupts the passivation regime (e.g., very aggressive pH or chloride concentrations), the beneficial effects may not be observed.
generation.uncertainty: While available evidence supports that microstructural control (grain refinement and precipitate formation) enhances separate wear and corrosion properties, the detailed extent of synergistic improvement under simultaneous attack is not precisely quantified. Variations in alloy chemistry beyond processing-induced microstructure might also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples with identical chemical compositions but different microstructures via controlled sintering: one with a refined grain structure and continuous grain-boundary precipitates (low-temperature sintering) and one with a coarser structure and discontinuous precipitates (high-temperature sintering). Subject both sets to simultaneous wear and corrosion tests in a corrosive acidic (e.g., H2SO4) electrolyte while applying a controlled abrasive load. Perform electrochemical measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) and mechanical wear tests (e.g., sliding wear tests).
measurements: Passivation film stability (via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined microstructure with continuous precipitates does not exhibit statistically lower wear and corrosion rates compared to the coarser baseline, or if results show no significant improvement in the integrated resistance under combined degradation, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. The CrMoNbWV HEA has comparable mechanical and corrosive properties with the WNbMoTaV type HEA, but at the same time has a reduced density: CrMoNbWV—10.55 g/cm

Abstract The growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
